column2: Quick question. What's eighty-five squared?
Seven thousand two hundred twenty-five. Eight times nine is seventy-two. Then write twenty-five.
If that took you longer than four seconds, there's a likely reason. The usual way to multiply is built for paper. For this one, that's two rows of digits and three carries.
On paper that's fine, because the paper remembers the rows. In your head, you have to hold both rows while you add them.
The trick holds one number. Seventy-two.
And it rests on a picture. If you ever forget the trick, the picture gives it back. So every trick here comes with its picture. And there are problems for you to try.
Here's that trick on a smaller number. Thirty-five squared. The number in front of the five is three.
Multiply it by the next number up. Three times four is twelve.
Then write twenty-five after it. One thousand two hundred twenty-five.
But why the next number up, and not three times three?
Thirty-five squared is the area of a square, thirty-five on each side. Slice a strip off the top, five deep.
Now turn the strip, and stand it against the side.
The square has become a rectangle. Five shorter, so thirty tall. Five wider, so forty wide. And the end of the strip sticks up. A small square, five by five.
Thirty by forty is three times four, in hundreds. Twelve hundred.
And the small square is the twenty-five. Twelve hundred plus twenty-five. The next number comes in because thirty-five sits halfway between thirty and forty.
Your turn. Whenever you want more time, pause the video. What's twenty-five squared?
Two times three is six. Then twenty-five. Six hundred twenty-five.
It works for every whole number that ends in five, because two things never change. Whatever is in front, the strip is five deep and the small square is twenty-five.
In letters, call the number in front n. Multiply it by the next number, for the hundreds. Then add twenty-five.
It's only as easy as that one multiplication, though. One hundred thirty-five squared needs thirteen times fourteen. We'll come back for that.
Most problems aren't that neat. Take twenty-three times forty-six. Before anything else, round first. Twenty times fifty is a thousand, so the answer is near a thousand.
Now draw it. A rectangle, twenty-three by forty-six. Its area is the answer.
Break each number into parts. Twenty and three. Forty and six. The rectangle falls into four pieces. A big block, two strips and a small corner.
Take the block, twenty by forty. Two times four is eight. But is that eighty, eight hundred, or eight thousand?
Eight hundred. Twenty times four is eighty already, so twenty times forty has to be ten times that. Tens times tens are hundreds.
So leave the zeros out while you multiply, and put them back by asking how big the piece has to be.
The other three go the same way. Twenty times six, one hundred twenty. Three times forty, one hundred twenty again, which is rare. Three times six, eighteen.
Four easy multiplications. Now there are four numbers to hold while you add them.
Four numbers is a lot to hold. So don't hold them. Keep one running total, and add each piece the moment you have it.
Block, strip, strip, corner. Twenty times forty, eight hundred. Add twenty times six, nine hundred twenty. Add three times forty, one thousand forty. And three times six, one thousand fifty-eight.
Between steps, you only ever held one number. And each total was a floor, so the answer could only go up.
Your turn. Six times forty-three?
Six times forty, two hundred forty. Add six times three, eighteen. Two hundred fifty-eight.
And the one we left. It has four pieces, so pause if you like. Thirteen times fourteen?

Ten times ten, one hundred. Add ten times four, one hundred forty. Add three times ten, one hundred seventy. And three times four, one hundred eighty-two. Then twenty-five. One hundred thirty-five squared is eighteen thousand two hundred twenty-five.
Now money. A restaurant bill of forty-eight dollars, and you want to tip fifteen percent. Ten percent is one tenth, so the decimal point moves one place to the left. Four dollars eighty.
Five percent is half of that. Two dollars forty. Together, seven dollars twenty.
And twenty percent is the tenth, doubled. Seventeen percent already takes four pieces.
Your turn. Fifteen percent of sixty dollars?
A tenth is six dollars. Half of that is three dollars. Nine dollars.
What's eight percent of twenty-five dollars?
Swap the two numbers. Twenty-five percent of eight dollars is a quarter of eight. Two dollars. That's the answer to both.

Percent means cents on the dollar. Eight cents from each of twenty-five dollars. Or twenty-five cents from each of eight. The same two hundred cents. The swap pays when one side is a friendly percent, like a tenth, a quarter or a half.
Five is half of ten. So five times eighty-six is ten times eighty-six, cut in half. Eight hundred sixty, cut in half. Four hundred thirty.
The same cut works between two numbers. Fourteen times thirty-five. Take half of the fourteen, and double the thirty-five. Seven times seventy. Four hundred ninety.
Your turn. Sixteen times forty-five?
Half of one, double the other. Eight times ninety. Seven hundred twenty. It pays when doubling makes a round number. One of them even, the other ending in five.

Take a price just under a round number. Four things at nineteen dollars ninety-nine. Call it four times twenty, eighty dollars. Then give back four cents. Seventy-nine dollars ninety-six. That's round, then fix.
Your turn. Three things at four dollars ninety-nine each?
Three times five, fifteen dollars. Give back three cents. Fourteen dollars ninety-seven. This one pays when the fix is small. A round number close by, and only a few things to fix.
Forty-seven times fifty-three. Before you start on the parts, look at the two numbers. What number sits exactly halfway between them?
It's fifty, the middle. One is three below it, the other three above. A distance of three.
So draw fifty squared, and lay the rectangle over it. It sticks out by three at the side, and falls short by three at the top.
Move the strip that sticks out into the gap. It nearly fills it. What's missing is one small square, three by three.
So the answer is fifty squared, minus three squared. Twenty-five hundred, minus nine. Two thousand four hundred ninety-one.
Your turn. Nineteen times twenty-one?
The middle is twenty, and the distance is one. Four hundred, minus one. Three hundred ninety-nine.
It needs a middle and a distance that are both easy to square. Forty-seven times fifty-six has its middle at fifty-one and a half. Back to parts.

The next trick comes with a story. Los Alamos, in the nineteen forties, where the first atomic bomb was being built. Hans Bethe runs the Theoretical Division, and Richard Feynman works for him. They're working through a formula, and it calls for forty-eight squared.
Feynman turns to the calculator. Bethe already has an answer. Twenty-three hundred.
Feynman keys it in all the same. Bethe adds that the exact answer is twenty-three oh four.
Feynman calls it remarkable. And Bethe asks him a question. Don't you know how to square numbers near fifty?
Fifty squared is twenty-five hundred. How would you get from there to forty-eight squared?
Here's the picture, and it's the move from before. Forty-eight squared. Slice a strip off the top, two deep, and stand it against the side.
Now it's as wide as fifty squared, and four rows short. That's two hundred, a hundred for each one below fifty. And that's Bethe's twenty-three hundred.
And the end of the strip sticks up. Two by two. Plus four.
Now a number above fifty. What changes for fifty-three squared?
The same move. Slice off three, and stand it against the side.

Now it's fifty tall, and six columns wider than fifty squared. That's three hundred, a hundred for each one above fifty. And the end sticks up. Three by three is nine. Two thousand eight hundred nine.

Which gives a quick way to say it. Start from twenty-five. Above fifty, add the distance. Below fifty, take it off. That's the hundreds. Then write the distance squared, as two digits. Nine is oh nine.
Your turn. Forty-six squared?
Four below. Twenty-five minus four is twenty-one. Four squared is sixteen. Twenty-one sixteen.

That reads straight off while you're within nine of fifty. Further out, the distance squared runs past two digits, and it spills into the hundreds. Sixty-two is twelve above. Thirty-seven hundred, plus one hundred forty-four. Thirty-eight forty-four.

After that, Feynman took up tricks like these himself. He almost never got there before Bethe, who could get close to nearly any answer. And he tells us what made that easy. Every number was near something he knew.
Now they're mixed up, so the first job is to pick the trick. Pause whenever you like. A twenty percent tip on forty-five dollars?
Start from a tenth. Four dollars fifty. Doubled, nine dollars.
Forty-nine times fifty-one?
One either side of fifty. Twenty-five hundred, minus one. Two thousand four hundred ninety-nine.
Last one of this round. Sixty-seven times seventy-eight?
Nothing to grab. It doesn't end in five. Its middle is seventy-two and a half. And the nearest round number doesn't make it easy.
Parts still works, in four slow steps. Five thousand two hundred twenty-six.
That's four pieces with carrying, and it's slow. There's no shame in reaching for paper, or a calculator.

But keep one habit even then. Round first. Seventy times eighty is fifty-six hundred. If a calculator shows five hundred and something, or fifty thousand, something went wrong. That won't catch a small slip. It tells you how big the answer has to be.
One more, and it has a twist. Fifty-five squared?

It ends in five. Five times six is thirty, then twenty-five. It's also near fifty. Twenty-five plus five is thirty, then twenty-five. Thirty twenty-five, both ways. Any trick that fits gives the same answer.

They're the same move. Slice a strip off a square, stand it against the side, and you have a rectangle and a small square. Thirty times forty, plus twenty-five. Forty-six times fifty, plus four. And fifty squared is forty-seven times fifty-three, plus nine.
In letters, it's the line from the middle trick, with the small square moved across.

You don't need a gift for numbers for any of this. You need a few numbers you know well, and the habit of looking for one nearby. Every number is near something you know. Sometimes that gives you the answer. It always tells you how big the answer is.
